extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical exercises for creating believable, dimensional characters in fiction—covering desire, complexity, contrast, consistency, change, sources, and methods for showing character. Useful for short stories and novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire (driving force)
rubrics_metrics.description: One driving desire. Make the desire something concrete—money, a career break, the touch of a certain person—instead of an abstract desire like love or personal growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong desire makes the story line grow organically from the character's need; without desire a story will fizzle (example: student with descriptive mansion exploration). Examples: Humbert Humbert's craving for Lolita drives Nabokov's Lolita; Claire's desire to understand drives 'So Much Water So Close to Home.' Make desire specific and concrete to create momentum and tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human complexity (avoid flat types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is less compelling in a story than a character who acts like a million other characters you've encountered, exhibiting only one facet: the kindly grandma, the sinister janitor, the heroic patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcend types by exploring specific and unique details that make a character distinct (example: investment banker Richard also donates anonymously and calls his sister when drunk). Use small details (voice, habits, gestures) and larger decisions to show dimensionality (example: Connie in Oates's story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional villains / redeeming quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign one redeeming quality to an otherwise reprehensible or 'worst' character so they become fully dimensional rather than purely evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad characters aren't bad every second—give them small humane actions or traits (examples: a sadistic ex-spouse helping a homeless person; a bank robber arranging a babysitter). Allowing even a tiny bit of ourselves to be seen in villains makes them more compelling (example: Humbert Humbert's charm and intelligence). Exercise: recall the worst person you know and assign a redeeming quality, then write them in action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrasting traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters possess contrasting traits—sometimes subtle, other times greatly conflicting—and these contrasts provide endless opportunity to make characters complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show contrasts through behavior in different contexts (example: Connie's home vs. out-with-friends persona). Contrasts should be seamlessly sewn into characterization (not announced); they should seep into the narrative so the reader experiences tension rather than spotting obvious contrasts. Use unexpected or not-quite-matching qualities to add complexity without predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (believability)
rubrics_metrics.description: All actions and behaviors should seem authentic and true to the character based on what you have established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting qualities are moments of humanness, but overall characterization must be consistent. If a character does something 'out of character' the reader needs prior glimmers of that tendency (foreshadowing). Avoid abrupt, unexplained shifts; provide indications (dialogue, drinking, resentment) that make later extreme actions believable (example: Nick's mounting instability before he shoots his wife).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to change (arc potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should possess the ability to change, and the reader should see this potential; the choice to change should be present during the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change can be dramatic or a gentle realization and need not be complete by the end, but the reader must sense capacity for transformation (examples: Dmitry in 'The Lady with the Dog'; Humbert Humbert's partial change). If you don't create potential for change the character will feel predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source material for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters will emerge from people you know and see and even imagine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with interesting people, parts of yourself, or close observation; fictionalize real people rather than slavishly sticking to facts. Use 'what if?' to expand observed moments into situations for characterization (examples: weeping girl at bus stop, group at bar). Immerse in environments (example: Algren and Chicago) to ground characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting to know characters (developmental work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest time to get to know your characters as if they were good friends; put them in different scenarios to understand how they'd act and react.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider categories: Appearance, Background, Personality, Primary Identity. Run them through varied situations (e.g., accidental shoplifting, travel contexts) to reveal authentic behavior. This foundational intimacy lets you portray them with more authenticity on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed character questions (homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extensive, specific questions—both basic and unconventional—to build a deep well of knowledge about your character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample basic questions include name, hair/eye color, scars, friends/family, birthplace, biggest fear, secrets, loves. Unconventional questions probe refrigerator contents, what is on their nightstand, feet/clothing, childhood kitchen smell, what they can't throw away, Saturday noon routine, strong childhood memory, getting-ready-for-night-out details. You won't use all answers, but knowing them makes characters explicable (Forster quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of characters and appropriate depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all characters need equal development: protagonists need fullest development; secondary characters need a few defining details; extras can remain flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protagonist: full dimensionality (desire, complexity, contrast, consistency, change). Antagonist: person who poses obstacle (need not be 'bad'). Secondary characters: capture essence with a few defining details (example: Jordan as tennis player/gossipy). Extras: minimal dimension to avoid stealing focus. Understand round vs flat: round characters can surprise convincingly; flat characters serve limited roles effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling (when to tell, when to show)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two basic methods of revealing a character: showing and telling. Showing is generally more interesting; telling can be used efficiently for quick distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing gives readers more to engage with and creates momentum; telling is appropriate for quick introductions or distinctions (example: narrator's quick telling of Frankie Machine and Sparrow). Avoid overreliance on telling; prefer showing through specific details so reader interacts with the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four methods to show character
rubrics_metrics.description: Show character through: Action, Speech, Appearance, Thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action is usually the strongest method because it reveals how a character handles situations and makes traits observable (examples: how someone deals with a neighbor's garbage, Tuesday night habits, coping with a screaming man). Use a mix of the four to reveal dimensionality. Specific choices (what they drink, where they hide) convey nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles and concrete complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Place obstacles in the character's path to create tension and to reveal character while pursuing desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small or large obstacles (e.g., being trapped in an attic, attending an audition to which one is not invited) force action and show both contrasting traits and potential for change. Exercises encourage adding obstacles to a character's pursuit of a concrete desire to generate momentum and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show specifics (choose evocative details)
rubrics_metrics.description: When showing, find the specific details that will convey necessary information while keeping the reader's attention on emotion and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, evocative details (e.g., Greta experimenting with materials, sipping tea, preferring cavelike surroundings) suggest personality more powerfully than direct statements. Small sensory or behavioral items often reveal more than explicit description and make scenes more interesting to read.
